estonian_linda.name: Carry the stones of Kalev's grave-mound
estonian_linda.notes: In the epic Linda heaps up a great cairn over her dead husband Kalev; the stone she drops in grief at Lake Ülemiste is folk-aetiology of the lake's origin.

sources.reference: Kreutzwald, Kalevipoeg, Canto I

etruscan_aita.name: Rule the realm of the dead
etruscan_aita.notes: Enthroned lord of the Etruscan underworld, counterpart of Greek Hades/Pluthon, presiding with his consort Phersipnai over the souls of the deceased.

sources.reference: de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)

etruscan_aita.name: Pass unseen in the wolf-skin cap
etruscan_aita.notes: His wolf-skin headdress (a transformation of Hades' kyne, the dog-skin helmet of invisibility) marks his chthonic, unseen power over death.

sources.reference: de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)

etruscan_charun.name: Seal the door of death with the hammer
etruscan_charun.notes: Charun wields a great hammer or mallet, his defining attribute, to strike the threshold and confirm/seal a death; the blow consigns the soul to the underworld.

sources.reference: de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)

etruscan_charun.name: Escort the dead to the underworld
etruscan_charun.notes: As psychopomp he meets the newly dead and guides (rather than punishes) them to the world below, frequently paired with Vanth.

sources.reference: Krauskopf, in The Religion of the Etruscans (2006)

etruscan_fufluns.name: Quicken the vine and the growth of plants
etruscan_fufluns.notes: God of wine, plant-life, joy, health and growth; the Etruscan reception of Dionysos, namesake of Populonia (Fufluna).

sources.reference: Bonfante & Swaddling, Etruscan Myths (2006)

etruscan_fufluns.name: Grant ecstatic release and the promise of rebirth
etruscan_fufluns.notes: Lord of a mystery-cult (Fufluns Pacha) attended by satyrs and maenads, offering initiates ecstatic communion and the hope of an afterlife.

sources.reference: de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)

etruscan_laran.name: Command war and martial valour
etruscan_laran.notes: God of war, the Etruscan counterpart of Ares/Mars, shown as the armed defender; on the Populonia mirror he fights the giant Celsclan, son of the earth-goddess Cel.

sources.reference: de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)

etruscan_laran.name: Hurl the thunderbolt
etruscan_laran.notes: Counted among the nine Etruscan deities permitted to wield lightning.

sources.reference: de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)

etruscan_nethuns.name: Rule wells, springs and the sea
etruscan_nethuns.notes: Lord of fresh and salt water, of wells and springs, source of the Roman Neptune; named (as Neθ) on the Liver of Piacenza and the Liber Linteus.

sources.reference: Liver of Piacenza

etruscan_nethuns.name: Wield the thunderbolt
etruscan_nethuns.notes: Reckoned among the Etruscan gods empowered to hurl lightning, marking his rank among the great deities.

sources.reference: de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)

etruscan_persipnei.name: Reign as queen of the underworld
etruscan_persipnei.notes: Consort of Aita and queen of the dead, the Etruscan reception of Persephone/Proserpina, enthroned beside Aita in the painted tombs.

sources.reference: de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)

etruscan_selvans.name: Guard boundaries and the wild edges of cultivated land
etruscan_selvans.notes: Tutelary god of woodland, wilderness and boundary-stones (epithet tularias, 'of the boundaries'); a public cult deity at Volsinii, receiving dedications from women as well as men.

sources.reference: Liver of Piacenza

etruscan_sethlans.name: Work fire and the forge
etruscan_sethlans.notes: God of fire, the forge and metalworking, the Etruscan Hephaestus/Vulcan; first attested in the 4th c. BCE.

sources.reference: de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)

etruscan_sethlans.name: Cleave open Tinia's head to free Menrva
etruscan_sethlans.notes: On Etruscan mirrors he is the craftsman who splits Tinia's skull with his axe so that the armed Menrva may be born.

sources.reference: de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)

etruscan_tages.name: Reveal the Etrusca Disciplina
etruscan_tages.notes: Plowed from a furrow at Tarquinia with a child's body and a sage's wisdom, he dictated the rules of haruspicy and the reading of lightning, then died; the fountainhead of Etruscan sacred science (Cicero, De Divinatione II).

sources.reference: Cicero, De Divinatione 2.50

etruscan_thesan.name: Bring forth the dawn and the daylight
etruscan_thesan.notes: Goddess of the dawn, counterpart of Eos/Aurora, associated with birth and the coming of day; received offerings beside the sun-god Usil in the Liber Linteus.

sources.reference: Liber Linteus Zagrabiensis

etruscan_thesan.name: Carry off a mortal youth at daybreak
etruscan_thesan.notes: On 6th-5th c. BCE mirrors she abducts a young lover (e.g. Kephalos/Tithun), winged and nimbed, mirroring Eos and Tithonus.

sources.reference: de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)

etruscan_turan.name: Kindle love, desire and vitality
etruscan_turan.notes: Goddess of love, desire and fertility, the Etruscan Aphrodite/Venus and patron of Vulci; her lover is Atunis (Adonis) and her retinue the winged Lasas.

sources.reference: de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)

etruscan_vanth.name: Light the road of the dead with her torch
etruscan_vanth.notes: Winged female psychopomp who appears at the moment of death bearing a torch; indigenous to Etruria with no Greek counterpart, she guides rather than punishes.

sources.reference: de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)

etruscan_vanth.name: Know and announce the appointed fate
etruscan_vanth.notes: In the François Tomb she holds an open scroll recording the destiny of the dead, witnessing the doom of the Trojan captives.

sources.reference: François Tomb, Vulci, wall-paintings

ewe_lisa.name: Wield the strength and heat of day
ewe_lisa.notes: As the male, solar half of the creator pair Mawu-Lisa, Lisa embodies the sun, daytime, heat and strength, complementing Mawu's cool nocturnal moon.

sources.reference: Herskovits, Dahomey: An Ancient West African Kingdom (1938)

ewe_lisa.name: Order the created world with Mawu
ewe_lisa.notes: With Mawu, Lisa shapes and orders the cosmos from pre-existing matter, dividing day from night between the pair.

sources.reference: Herskovits, Dahomey: An Ancient West African Kingdom (1938)

fang_mebere.name: Establish order and governance
fang_mebere.notes: Second person of the Nzame-Mebere-Nkwa triad, the aspect of rule and order who with Nzame and Nkwa resolves to give the new earth a ruler.

sources.reference: Fernandez, Bwiti: An Ethnography of the Religious Imagination in Africa (1982)

ewe_da.gloss: the cosmic rainbow-serpent that upholds the world

sources.reference: Herskovits, Dahomey: An Ancient West African Kingdom (1938)
Egharevba, A Short History of Benin (1968)

fang_mebege.gloss: Zame, son of Mebege (firstborn of the creator)

sources.reference: Fernandez, Bwiti (1982)

estonian_tharapita.name: Pre-battle invocation of Tharapita
estonian_tharapita.notes: The Oeselians and Vironians cried out to Tharapita before battle, as recorded for the campaigns of 1217 and 1227 in the Chronicle of Henry of Livonia; his cult-place was the wooded Ebavere hill in Vironia.

sources.reference: Henry of Livonia, Chronicon Livoniae XXX.5

estonian_maaema.name: Midsummer offering to the Earth Mother
estonian_maaema.notes: Mothers carried food-offerings to sacrificial stones at Midsummer, saying 'Maaema, you gave it to me and now I bring it to you'; offerings were also laid under boundary stones to secure soil fertility.

sources.reference: Loorits, Grundzüge des estnischen Volksglaubens (1949)

estonian_pikker.name: Animal sacrifice to Pikne
estonian_pikker.notes: Medieval pagan priests offered animal sacrifices to the thunder-god; Pikne was held protector of the holy river Võhandu and withheld rain from those who dammed it for mills.

sources.reference: Eisen, Eesti mütoloogia (1919)

etruscan_fufluns.name: Mystery-cult of Fufluns Pacha
etruscan_fufluns.notes: An ecstatic mystery-cult at Vulci and Populonia, with maenadic and satyric celebrants, promising initiates rebirth; attested by Bacchic acclamations (paχies) inscribed on imported Attic vases.

sources.reference: Vulci inscriptions on Attic pottery, 5th-4th c. BCE

etruscan_uni.name: Cult of Uni-Astarte at Pyrgi
etruscan_uni.notes: A 6th-c. BCE sanctuary at Pyrgi, the port of Caere, dedicated to Uni and identified bilingually with Phoenician Astarte; the dedication of Thefarie Velianas is preserved on the gold Pyrgi tablets.

sources.reference: Pyrgi Tablets, c. 500 BCE

etruscan_thesan.name: Dawn-cult at Pyrgi
etruscan_thesan.notes: Worshipped at Caere's harbour of Pyrgi, where a temple yielded a distinctive series of 'daybreak' antefixes; she received offerings alongside the sun-god Usil in the Liber Linteus.

sources.reference: Liber Linteus Zagrabiensis

etruscan_selvans.name: Votive cult of Selvans
etruscan_selvans.notes: A public cult, especially of the tuthina of Volsinii, attested from the 5th c. BCE by votive bronze statuettes and objects inscribed to Selvans, set up by women as well as men.

sources.reference: Etruscan votive inscriptions to Selvans

ewe_so.name: Yeve thunder-cult
ewe_so.notes: The secretive Yeve (Yewe) order of the thunder-vodu among the Anlo-Ewe, with possession-dance, drumming and a long seclusion-initiation; its devotees serve as a ritual enforcer of social and moral order.

sources.reference: Rosenthal, Possession, Ecstasy, and Law in Ewe Voodoo (1998)

ewe_afa.name: Afa divination
ewe_afa.notes: Casting the sixteen palm-kernels (deki) or the divining chain (agumaga) to read one of the 256 signs (du / kpoli), revealing the destiny set by Mawu and the taboos binding the initiate's life.

sources.reference: Maupoil, La géomancie à l'ancienne Côte des Esclaves (1943)

ewe_sakpata.name: Earth-and-pox cult of Sakpata
ewe_sakpata.notes: A powerful priesthood owning the earth and smallpox, its initiates clothed in raffia hood and skirt; bound by strict taboos to send or withdraw the eruptive fevers from the unappeased or appeased.

sources.reference: Herskovits, Dahomey: An Ancient West African Kingdom (1938)

ewuare_great.name: Igue festival
ewuare_great.notes: Instituted by Ewuare to renew the Oba's mystical powers and bless his head and the kingdom; the king dances with the Eben sword in full coral regalia. The associated Ugie Ewere re-enacts his marriage to Ewere.

sources.reference: Egharevba, A Short History of Benin (1968)

attributes.name: Grey-bearded elder
attributes.notes: Depicted in romantic-era Estonian art as a grey-bearded old singer, the 'Estonian Orpheus', after the Finnish Väinämöinen.

sources.reference: Viires, 'Pseudomythology in Estonian Publicity' (1991)

attributes.name: Bearded enthroned king in wolf-skin cap
attributes.notes: Mature bearded figure crowned with a wolf-skin headdress, enthroned beside Phersipnai in the painted tombs.

sources.reference: Tomb of Orcus II, Tarquinia, wall-paintings
Tomb of Orcus II, Tarquinia, wall-paintings

attributes.name: Blue-fleshed bestial demon
attributes.notes: Bluish, decaying skin, hooked vulture's nose, tusks, pointed ears and great wings, brandishing a hammer.

sources.reference: Monterozzi Tomb 5636, Tarquinia, wall-painting
Monterozzi Tomb 5636, Tarquinia, wall-painting

attributes.name: Beardless youth with satyrs and maenads
attributes.notes: Usually a beardless young man (rarely an older bearded figure) amid his thiasos of satyrs and maenads.

sources.reference: Bonfante & Swaddling, Etruscan Myths (2006)
Bonfante & Swaddling, Etruscan Myths (2006)
Bonfante & Swaddling, Etruscan Myths (2006)

attributes.name: Naked helmeted youth with spear and shield
attributes.notes: A youthful warrior, often nude but for helmet and cuirass, gripping spear and shield, as in the Mars of Todi bronze.

sources.reference: Mars of Todi bronze, Vatican Museums

attributes.name: Sea-monster (ketos) headdress with trident
attributes.notes: On the Vetulonia coin his profile wears a ketos headdress, his trident set between two dolphins.

sources.reference: Coin of Vetulonia, c. 215-211 BCE
Coin of Vetulonia, c. 215-211 BCE

attributes.name: Enthroned queen with snakes in her hair
attributes.notes: Shown enthroned beside Aita, snakes entwined in her hair, holding a bird-topped scepter.

sources.reference: Golini Tomb I, Orvieto, and Tomb of Orcus II, Tarquinia
Tomb of Orcus II, Tarquinia, wall-paintings

attributes.name: Naked youth in bear-skin cap and high boots
attributes.notes: The single certain image shows him as a nude youth wearing a cap of bear-hide and high boots, unlike the Roman Silvanus.

sources.reference: de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)

attributes.name: Smith in conical workman's cap (pileus)
attributes.notes: Identified by hammer, tongs and double axe and by the conical workman's cap (pileus).

sources.reference: Historical Dictionary of the Etruscans, s.v. Sethlans

attributes.name: Child with the wisdom of a seer
attributes.notes: A boy's body bearing a sage's wisdom, risen from the furrow; named Tarchies on the Tuscania mirror.

sources.reference: Tuscania bronze mirror

attributes.name: Winged, nimbed dawn-goddess in flight
attributes.notes: Winged and sometimes haloed, shown running or flying as she carries off a youthful lover.

sources.reference: Etruscan mirror, Museo Gregoriano Etrusco (Thesan and Kephalos)

attributes.name: Young winged girl with her Lasas
attributes.notes: A youthful winged goddess, in early art richly robed and jewelled, later nude under Hellenistic influence, attended by the winged Lasas.

sources.reference: de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)
de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)
de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)

attributes.name: Winged female in hunting-boots with torch
attributes.notes: A great-winged young woman, often bare-breasted (apotropaic), in hunting-boots, bearing torch, key and scroll and brandishing snakes.

sources.reference: de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)
de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)
de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)
de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)
de Grummond, Etruscan Myth, Sacred History, and Legend (2006)

attributes.name: Half-man, half-bear hunter
attributes.notes: The first-ancestor depicted as half man, half bear, pursuing the cosmic elk; in the sky he is figured by Boötes/Arcturus.

sources.reference: Anisimov, in Studies in Siberian Shamanism (1963)
Anisimov, in Studies in Siberian Shamanism (1963)

attributes.name: Antlered cosmic cow-elk
attributes.notes: The great elk (Kheglun) whose body forms the bowl of Ursa Major, bearing the sun away on her antlers each night, her calf the stars of Ursa Minor.

sources.reference: Antonello, 'The myths of the Bear' (2013)
Antonello, 'The myths of the Bear' (2013)

attributes.name: Ram with lightning from its mouth
attributes.notes: Manifest as a ram (sometimes painted red), lightning issuing from its mouth, its curved horns likened to the bolt and the clash of rams to thunder; flanked by two curved thunder-axes.

sources.reference: Herskovits, Dahomey: An Ancient West African Kingdom (1938)
Herskovits, Dahomey: An Ancient West African Kingdom (1938)

attributes.name: Phallic mound-figure painted red, white and black
attributes.notes: Represented by a clay mound or small figure with a prominent phallus, set at the doorway and crossroads.

sources.reference: Herskovits, Dahomey: An Ancient West African Kingdom (1938)
Herskovits, Dahomey: An Ancient West African Kingdom (1938)

attributes.name: Iron blade and forge
attributes.notes: Manifest in iron itself; his cult-object is an assemblage of iron blades, and his symbol the cutlass.

sources.reference: Herskovits, Dahomey: An Ancient West African Kingdom (1938)
Blier, African Vodun: Art, Psychology, and Power (1995)

attributes.name: Raffia hood and skirt, red-and-white spots
attributes.notes: Devotees clothed head to foot in raffia; the god marked by black, white and red spots evoking the pocks of smallpox.

sources.reference: Herskovits, Dahomey: An Ancient West African Kingdom (1938)

attributes.name: Rainbow-coloured serpent biting its tail
attributes.notes: A great serpent arching as the rainbow and coiled in the sea, often shown biting its own tail, encircling and upholding the world.

sources.reference: Herskovits, Dahomey: An Ancient West African Kingdom (1938)
Herskovits, Dahomey: An Ancient West African Kingdom (1938)

attributes.name: Oba in coral-bead regalia
attributes.notes: Robed in coral crowns, shirts, aprons and necklaces (said to have been taken from Olokun), giving the Oba a god-like appearance.

sources.reference: Ben-Amos, The Art of Benin (1995)

attributes.name: Child who grows to a man in days
attributes.notes: Born of a Lakota mother who fell from the Star Country, he matures within a few years into a monster-slaying hero.

sources.reference: Walker, Lakota Belief and Ritual (1980)
